1:
The chapter opens as a soliloquy, and the first question is who speaks. Charles Ellicott notes that the Jewish Targum and many modern critics hear only the voice of the prophet, but himself recognises the ideal Servant, the view the Lord’s own use of the passage suggests. John Gill canvasses the same authorities and comes down harder still. The Targum makes them the prophet’s words about himself, and Aben Ezra and Kimchi say so too, though Kimchi elsewhere calls them the Messiah’s; Gill has no doubt that the Messiah is the speaker. What rested on him, he adds, was not the gifts of the Spirit only but the person of the Spirit, the third person in the Trinity, seen upon him by the baptist, qualifying him as man and Mediator. John Wesley holds the middle ground: the prophet may speak of himself, but the words are principally to be understood of Christ. Adam Clarke makes that duality a rule of the book: in most of these prophecies there is a primary and a secondary sense, a remote subject illustrated by one near, and the deliverance from Babylon constantly shadows forth a greater salvation; the prophet is himself a typical person, and the passage refers at once to his preaching and the Lord’s.

Two textual notes follow, and on the second the voices divide. Clarke reports that the Greek and Latin versions, the gospel quotation and three other witnesses omit the second divine name, which he thinks was inserted to prevent the pronouncing of the name that follows. On the clause about the prison he cites manuscripts collated by Kennicott and De Rossi, one of his own and the Complutensian, which write two words as one, a reading the old versions appear to have followed, giving not merely the opening of prisons but every kind of liberty; and he hears in the proclamation an allusion to the year of jubilee, a general release of debts, of bondmen and of lands. Ellicott takes the prison clause the other way: the Greek version, adopted in the gospel, gives recovery of sight to the blind, and since the verb is never used of a room or a door but is used elsewhere of the eyes, that is probably its meaning. He adds that the anointing might be that of a king, a priest or a prophet, and as interpreted by its fulfilment may include all three, and that the thought in binding up the broken-hearted is a bandage applied to the wounds of the heart, the Servant being physician as well as evangelist. He traces to this passage above all others the use of the word gospel.

Matthew Henry yields the exposition to another: the best expositor of scripture has given the best exposition here, our Lord himself, who read this in the synagogue at Nazareth and applied it entirely to himself. As the prophet proclaimed liberty to the captives, so Christ was to publish a more joyful jubilee to a lost world. The prophets had the Spirit moving them at times; Christ had it always without measure, and communicated it to those he sent with the same tidings. What service God called him to he furnished him for, setting him apart by a solemn unction, as kings and priests were of old. Three works follow: a preacher of good tidings to the meek, the penitent, the poor in spirit; a healer sent to bind up the broken-hearted, as broken bones are bound up that they may close again; and a deliverer proclaiming as a king. Wesley reads the anointing as a setting apart that capacitates with gifts and commissions with authority, and adds a power to make all effectual, whence the name Messiah among the Hebrews and Christ among the Greeks: he assigns the proclaimed liberty to the kingly office, from the dominion of sin and the fear of hell.
2:
John Gill begins by denying that the acceptable year is a year. It means time in general, and those are wrong who infer that the ministry of Christ lasted only a year, since by the passovers he kept it must have been three or four; the phrase may take in the whole Gospel dispensation. The allusion is to the year of jubilee, with its proclamation of liberty, its release of debts and its restoration of inheritances; and since that proclamation fell on the day of atonement, Gill reports a Jewish interpreter who reads it as a year of reconciliation, and notes that it may also be rendered the year of God’s good will. Charles Ellicott allows that the jubilee is perhaps still in the prophet’s mind, but says the chief point is the contrast between a year of favour and a single day of vengeance. John Wesley justifies the vengeance as necessary, since where God delivers his people he must take vengeance on their enemies, chiefly the spiritual ones. Keil and Delitzsch work on the words: the phrase for proclaiming liberty is the law’s own term for the freedom of the jubilee, which fell every fiftieth year, and the noun comes from a stem denoting the swift flight of a swallow and free motion generally. They add that the difficult word for release is written as two, and that the Targum renders the first as an imperative, come to the light, though the second half is no Hebrew word.

At the third verse two explanations of one difficulty are opposed. Adam Clarke holds that a word necessary to the sense has been lost, of which the ancient versions preserve no traces, and follows a conjecture of Houbigant supplying the word for gladness from a line below, where it stands opposed to sorrow as the lost word stood opposed to mourners. Ellicott accounts for the gap without any loss: the verb, which means simply to set, has no object at all, and it seems the prophet corrected himself while writing, substituting for a word that would have suited only the coronet one better fitted to the whole context. Clarke renders the clause a beautiful crown instead of ashes, and explains the custom: in mourning, sackcloth was worn and ashes spread on the head, while splendid clothing and ointment were signs of joy. He calls the pairing of the two Hebrew words a play on sound this prophet often uses. Ellicott renders it a diadem taking the place of the ashes sprinkled on the head of mourners, says the assonance deserves notice, and observes that the noun behind the spirit of heaviness is the one used of dimly burning flax.

On the closing image Ellicott is precise: the trees are strictly terebinths or oaks, symbols of unfading verdure, the righteousness thought of as the gift of the Spirit and therefore enduring, manifesting his glory in their strength. Clarke renders them trees approved, oaks of righteousness or truth, whose flourishing condition should show that they were of God’s planting and the work of his hands. Wesley reads them as firm and well rooted, engrafted into Christ by faith; and he takes the surrounding figures as a set, ashes standing for whatever is proper to days of mourning and beauty for whatever becomes times of rejoicing, the oil of joy named from the anointings used at glad times and the garment from festival ornaments, since they had clothing appropriated to their conditions. Gill dwells on the mourners, who mourn for the corruptions of doctrine in Zion, the neglect of her ordinances, her divisions and the lukewarmness of many professors; and he traces the comfort appointed them from its ordering in counsel and covenant, through the promises and the charge to ministers to speak comfortably, to the Spirit who puts comfort into hearts that through unbelief refuse to be comforted.
4:
Matthew Henry reads the promises as made to those newly returned from captivity and extended to the gospel church and all delivered from spiritual thraldom. Their cities shall be raised out of the ruins in which they had long lain, and desolations it was feared would never be repaired shall be raised up. An unsanctified soul, he adds, is like a city broken down and without walls, which the gospel fits to be a habitation of God. John Gill takes the builders to be the captives set at liberty, and though the words were literally true at the return from Babylon, refers them chiefly to the forming of churches in the Gentile world, where there had been neither preaching nor ordinances. Charles Ellicott renders the phrase the waste places of olden time, and parts company with commentators who supply strangers as the subject: the prophet seems to look on the rebuilding as the people’s own work, service of another kind being assigned to the aliens. Adam Clarke thinks a word has dropped out here too, and would add after the verb the clause they that spring from thee, on manuscript authority and a parallel place with the very same sentence; he doubts also that the desolations of many generations can refer to the exile, which did not last so long, and suggests the later dispersion.

The fifth verse turns to the strangers, and the voices differ over who they are. Ellicott takes them as servants waiting for their master’s orders, and finds the implied thought to be that the whole people is raised to a priestly caste, leaving the world’s rough work to foreigners on a lower level. Henry takes it more gently: those lately servants shall now have servants, not of their brethren, who are all the Lord’s freemen, but of the strangers, who shall keep their sheep, till their ground and dress their gardens, the ancient employments of Abel, Cain and Adam: and he turns it inward: when by grace we attain a holy indifference to this world, the sons of the alien become our ploughmen and vinedressers. Clarke and Gill both read the strangers as Gentile ministers who shall preach Christ and feed the congregations with sound doctrine; John Wesley lets the name cover either Gentile converts or such as have only an outward profession, the flocks being churches fed with the word and the ploughmen a spiritual husbandry.

At the sixth verse the priesthood is widened. Gill reports an older reading which made the builders and ploughmen themselves the priests here named, but prefers to take it of the people when converted, with no distinction of priests and people but all made a royal priesthood, the ceremonial sacrifices being at an end. Ellicott sets it in a longer line: this had been the original ideal of the nation’s life, forfeited for a time and fulfilled at last in the citizens of the new Jerusalem; and as the people had succeeded to the place of the sons of Aaron, so mankind at large is to occupy the place of the people. Henry observes that those whom God sets at liberty he sets to work, his service being perfect freedom and the greatest honour, priests having been the peers of princes; Wesley says the whole body shall now be as near to God as the priests were. The seventh verse is the most damaged in the chapter. Clarke calls the received translation very confused and the Hebrew probably corrupted, takes his rendering from the Syriac, and notes that the first half of the verse is omitted in all printed copies of the Greek. Ellicott reads the double as compensation for the suffering of years, passing into a double inheritance of territory; Keil and Delitzsch say the shame of banishment will be changed into an excess of joy; and Gill promises double honour in things civil and religious.
8:
The eighth verse turns on a single clause about robbery, and the voices are not agreed on what it says. Charles Ellicott sets the received rendering aside. The words are commonly applied as condemning the formal sacrifices of the wicked, but so taken they do not fit the context, and he prefers what the Septuagint and the Targum give, that God hates robbery with violence, referring the phrase to the spoliation the people had suffered at the hands of their conquerors. Adam Clarke reaches nearly the same place by the letters. The Syriac and the Chaldee prefix a conjunction where the received text has a preposition, and render the following word iniquity or oppression, as the Septuagint does; the difference, he points out, lies wholly in the punctuation, since the consonants of the two readings are identical, and five of De Rossi’s manuscripts confirm it. Ellicott corrects the next clause as well: the word rendered work stands, as it does elsewhere in the law, for the reward of work, so that the promise is better read, I will appoint their recompense in faithfulness. John Wesley keeps the older sense throughout, taking the robbery as all things gotten by injustice even when brought for sacrifice, and the direction as a leading that will make them do all things in sincerity; on the covenant he is emphatic, that though they have broken covenant with God he will renew the ancient one made with their fathers, confirmed with the blood of Christ and never to be abrogated.

John Gill takes the love of judgment two ways. It means that God will do right himself and see it done by others, and so will right the wrongs of a people reproached and abused beyond measure among those they were scattered among; and it means also that he loves strict justice and real righteousness, and will not be put off with an imperfect righteousness in the room of a perfect one, still less with an insincere and hypocritical one. Nothing less is acceptable to him, Gill says, than a righteousness adequate to the demands of law and justice, and such a righteousness is not to be found among men but only in his Son. Wesley makes the same point more briefly, that God loves justice in himself and in those who practise it.

At the ninth verse the promise is of a seed known among the nations, and the question is what the knowing amounts to. Ellicott glosses it as renowned, or honourably recognised, even by the heathen, as the people whom the Lord has blessed. Gill expects not only a conversion of the people as a body in the latter day but a succession of converts in later ages, known among Christian Gentiles by their faith and love and good works and acknowledged by them as brethren. Clarke presses a point the others do not raise. Both are to make but one fold under one shepherd; yet they may still retain their peculiarity and national distinction, so that though they are known to be Christians they shall appear to be converted Jews, and this will necessarily be the case for a long time, since strange nations are not so speedily amalgamated as to lose their peculiar cast of features and their other national distinctions. Wesley offers two readings of the clause and refuses to choose: it may be a promise of the increase of the church, whose prosperity and multiplying will make it known abroad, or it may mean that the church, hitherto confined to one corner of the world, shall remain in one nation no more but fill all the nations of the earth. On the last words he adds that there shall be such visible characters of the love of God towards them, and of his grace in them, that the blessing will not need to be argued.
10:
The chapter ends in a song, and the first question is again who sings it. John Gill rules out two candidates first: these are not the words of the prophet in his own person, nor of Christ, but of the church, and especially of the Jewish church, expressing her joy for the benefits already declared. Charles Ellicott hears the same voice that opened the chapter, the ideal Servant identifying himself with the people, and notes that the Targum makes the city the speaker instead. Adam Clarke takes them for the words of converted Jews brought into the church of Christ and made fellow heirs with the Gentiles, and John Wesley says simply that it is spoken in the person of the church. Matthew Henry reports both older opinions, that some make it a song sung by the prophet in the name of the city, congratulating her on the change in her circumstances, and others make it spoken by Christ in the name of the New Testament church; and he declines to choose, taking the first as a type of the second. He adds that those who rejoice in God have cause to rejoice greatly, and that we need not fear running into an extreme in the greatness of our joy when we make God the gladness of it.

On the clothing the voices converge. Henry observes that those only shall be clothed with the garments of salvation hereafter who are covered with the robe of righteousness now; Christ has clothed his church with an eternal salvation by clothing it with the righteousness both of justification and sanctification, so that its members are decked as a bride to be espoused to God and as a priest to be employed for him. Wesley puts the figure in a line, salvation worn as a garment and righteousness as a robe. The comparison that follows is more technical than it looks. Clarke would render it as the bridegroom decketh himself with a priestly crown, an allusion to the dress of the high priest in his functions, and particularly to the mitre with its plate of gold in front, the priestly bonnet having been made, as the law expresses it, for glory and for beauty; he judges the metaphor difficult to carry into another language and thinks the versions of Aquila and Symmachus come nearest. Ellicott says the same more plainly, that the bridegroom literally wears a turban as a priest does, bridegrooms having apparently worn a special head-dress on the day of their espousal.

The last verse changes the figure from a wedding to a field, and Henry marks the point of the change: this is not like a day of triumph, which is glorious for the present but soon over, for the righteousness and salvation with which the church is clothed are durable clothing, springing forth for ages to come as the fruits of the earth are produced year after year. Gill fills in the picture, the tender grass of the spring after a long and cold winter, on ground that has been well manured. Wesley reads the promise as the breaking out of the great work of salvation, with praise as its natural fruit, and Ellicott finds the passage memorable as suggesting the leading thought of the parable of the sower and the title the Son of Man took from it. Clarke closes the chapter as he opened it, on the text rather than the sense. The second divine name here makes the line longer than those before and after, and the Septuagint and other old versions do not render it, so that a scholar he cites judged it interpolated; three manuscripts lack it, and in one of his own both words are wanting and supplied in the margin by a later hand.
